strengths: Clear problem formulation: the paper targets a genuine and under-explored weakness of REC models (distinguishing visually similar objects with different referring expressions), and the proposed image-space contrastive framework directly addresses it.

The core method is well motivated: using the ground-truth count N to assign top-N tokens as positives, plus the modified supervised contrastive loss that uses only positive anchors, is a sensible and clean adaptation of SupCon (Khosla et al.) to the REC setting; the theoretical/intuitive justification for the choice of N is additionally supported by ablations (Table 5) and supplementary analysis (~80% correct selections).

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art on REC-8K (4.86/13.60 MAE/RMSE val, 5.06/17.53 test) with clear margins over GroundingREC, plus competitive class-agnostic counting on FSC-147 (best text-based method) and CARPK, demonstrating the claimed generality.

The analysis of SOTA detection-based counting models identifying centroid (rather than bounding box) prediction as the key success factor is an interesting, actionable insight, backed by a component ablation (Table 6) and used to build a simple competitive baseline.

Thorough evaluation: results by object count range, by attribute category, qualitative comparisons including failure cases in the supplementary, and ablations covering the loss modification, number of selections, and baseline components.
Good clarity overall; the paper is well organized, the method section is precise (losses, token selection, thresholds, hyperparameters), and code is promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Much of the reported improvement comes from the new centroid-based baseline rather than the contrastive module itself: the 'GDino improved' baseline already beats GroundingREC on MAE/RMSE (5.90/19.73 vs 6.50/19.79 test), while the contrastive loss contributes a more modest additional gain (5.90→5.06 test MAE). The narrative as 'improving contrastive learning' somewhat oversells the relative contribution; the attribution should be more carefully separated.

Evaluation on a single REC benchmark (REC-8K), which was introduced by the closest prior work (GroundingREC/Dai et al.); the design choices (thresholds, N-selection, loss weights) may be implicitly tuned to this dataset. Additional REC evaluation, or at least a discussion, would strengthen generalization claims.

Positive pseudo-labels are formed by the N most similar tokens to the masked referring expression; this ~80% selection accuracy means roughly 20% of positives are misassigned, which the authors argue is tolerable, but no experiment directly measures sensitivity to selection noise (e.g., oracle vs. similarity selection) beyond the Table 5 alternatives.

In class-agnostic counting the gains are marginal and the proposed method is actually outperformed by the authors' own simpler baseline on CARPK (4.21/6.12 vs 3.80/5.16), weakening the 'versatile and generic' claim to some degree.

Writing issues: broken citations in the supplementary ([? ? ?]) where theoretical justification of the label-noise argument is claimed; duplicated/incorrect bibliography entries ([41] and [42] are the same paper); a few typos ('Noteably', 'choise'); inconsistent description of improvement (22% in abstract vs 1.4 points in contributions).

No limitations or societal-impact discussion; potential limitations such as reliance on a heavy pre-trained detector (Grounding DINO), inference-time thresholding hyperparameters, and behavior in extremely dense scenes (only 57 test samples with 100+ objects) are not explicitly acknowledged.

The novelty is incremental in components: supervised contrastive learning, Grounding DINO fine-tuning, and centroid regression each exist; the contribution is their combination and the anchor-modified SupCon loss, which is reasonable but modest as an algorithmic contribution.

strengths: C-REX achieves clear state-of-the-art results on the REC-8K benchmark (MAE 4.86/5.06 vs. 6.80/6.50 for the previous best GroundingREC), with consistent gains across object-count ranges (Fig. 3) and attribute categories (Fig. 4).

The core idea—performing supervised contrastive learning entirely in image space using the ground-truth count N to define positives, thereby avoiding image-text misalignment and enlarging the negative pool—is sensible and well-motivated relative to Dai et al.'s image-text contrastive scheme.

The paper includes a reasonably thorough ablation suite: the modified positive-anchor-only supervised loss (Table 4), the choice of N as the number of selections vs. alternatives (Table 5), and component analysis of the baseline (Table 6).

The analysis identifying centroid prediction (rather than bounding-box regression) as the key ingredient behind recent detection-based counting successes is a useful, verifiable observation, and the improved baseline itself is competitive.
Code availability is stated, and the method is largely reproducible from the implementation details (frozen Grounding DINO backbones, finetuned decoder, loss weights, thresholds).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is a modest modification of Khosla et al.'s supervised contrastive loss (restricting anchors to positives) applied on top of an existing detector (Grounding DINO), with pseudo-labels from top-N similarity to masked referring-expression tokens. The 'novel contrastive framework' framing overstates what is, in substance, a small loss tweak plus a strong baseline.

Attribution of gains is muddied: the improved baseline alone (GDino improved, 5.90/19.73 test) already outperforms the prior SOTA GroundingREC (6.50/19.79) without any contrastive component, and Table 6 shows GroundingREC minus feature fusion (6.16 MAE test) is close to the baseline. The abstract's headline '22% MAE / 10% RMSE' improvement substantially conflates the baseline redesign with the contrastive contribution; the contrastive loss itself accounts for roughly 0.84 MAE on the test set. The contribution list even states '1.4 points MAE,' which is inconsistent with the abstract's framing.

Evaluation is thin: REC results are on a single dataset (REC-8K), results appear to come from single runs with no variance or significance testing, and the class-agnostic extension is actually weaker than the authors' own baseline on CARPK (4.21 vs. 3.80 MAE), undercutting the 'general and versatile' claim.

Reliance on ground-truth count N to select positives is a potentially fragile supervision signal; the supplementary justification is qualitative ('approximately 80% of selected samples correspond to correct instances'), appeals to undefined citations that render as broken references ('[? ? ?]'), and the promised 'theoretical' justification is not substantiated.

Presentation quality issues: duplicated reference ([41] and [42] are the same paper), typos ('choise', 'Noteably'), inconsistent naming (GDino improved / GDino impr. / GREC), and a broken-reference passage in the supplementary suggesting incomplete proofreading.

The modification L*_sup is close to prior practice (anchor-only supervised contrastive objectives); no comparison to other natural alternatives (e.g., simply weighting negatives per class, or using GT point annotations directly as pseudo-labels instead of top-N similarity) is provided, so the design choices are not convincingly isolated.

No discussion of limitations or societal impact, and failure cases are only shown qualitatively in the supplementary without analysis of when/why the method breaks (e.g., text-based attribute understanding such as the 'T bottle cap' case).

strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results on REC: C-REX outperforms GroundingREC by a clear margin on REC-8K (test MAE 5.06 vs 6.50, RMSE 17.53 vs 19.79, best F1 0.70), with improvements shown across all object-count ranges (Fig. 3) and most attribute categories (Fig. 4), which substantiates the core claim.

The proposed image-space supervised contrastive loss with top-N pseudo-positive selection and positives-only anchoring is a well-motivated and simple modification of SupCon, and its design choices are empirically validated (Table 4 for the loss modification, Table 5 for the number of selections, including sensible alternatives like top-N+√N and top-N+2log2(N)).

Useful analysis contribution: identifying centroid prediction (rather than bounding box regression) as the key factor behind recent detection-based counting successes, supported by an ablation disentangling feature fusion and CL components of GroundingREC (Table 6). The resulting improved Grounding DINO baseline is itself valuable.

Demonstrated generality: the framework transfers to class-agnostic counting, where it is competitive with or better than prior text-based methods on FSC-147 (10.01 MAE), with an honest acknowledgment that gains are smaller in that setting.

Good experimental hygiene overall: comparison against retrained CountGD, reporting of F1 alongside MAE/RMSE, qualitative examples including failure cases in the supplementary, and a stated code release supporting reproducibility.
Clear writing and organization; the distinction from GroundingREC's image-text contrastive learning (larger negative pool, no cross-modal misalignment) is well argued.
weaknesses: Inconsistent improvement claims: the abstract states 'more than 22% in MAE and more than 10% in RMSE' while the contributions list 'over 1.4 points in MAE and over 2 points in RMSE'; these do not reconcile (relative vs. absolute framing is never clarified), which weakens the precision of the headline claim.

Attribution of gains between the improved baseline and the contrastive module deserves more scrutiny: the GDino-improved baseline alone (5.92/5.90 MAE) already beats GroundingREC, so a substantial portion of the reported SOTA margin comes from the baseline redesign rather than C-REX. The delta from the CL module (~1 point MAE) is meaningful but much smaller than the headline numbers suggest.

The pseudo-labeling procedure has a potential confirmation-bias issue: positives are selected via the model's own current similarity scores and then used as contrastive targets, which could reinforce initial errors. The supplementary analysis (80% selection accuracy) is helpful but qualitative and relies on broken citations ('[? ? ?]'), leaving the robustness of the choice under-reasoned, especially for cases with many visually confusable objects (N << Ñ).

Versatility claims are only partially supported: on CARPK, C-REX (4.21/6.12) actually underperforms the authors' own simpler baseline (3.80/5.16), and FSC-147 improvements over prior text-based methods are modest. The 'general and versatile' framing is somewhat stronger than the evidence.

Evaluation for REC is confined to a single dataset (REC-8K); no cross-dataset or out-of-distribution REC evaluation is provided, so generalization of the contrastive benefit beyond this benchmark is unverified.

Technical novelty is incremental: the loss is a relatively straightforward adaptation of supervised contrastive learning with an anchor restriction, and the baseline is a re-purposing of Grounding DINO; the paper's value rests mainly on empirical and analytical contributions rather than a new methodological idea.

Presentation issues: several typos ('Noteably', 'choise', 'leverages'), a missing url placeholder for the code link, broken references in the supplementary, and duplicative reference entries ([41]/[42]) should be corrected.

strengths: The core insight—shifting contrastive supervision from the image-text space to the visual embedding space for REC—is well-motivated and clearly argued; the analysis of why image-text CL is limited (few negatives, misalignment) is convincing and well-referenced.

Strong empirical validation: C-REX is evaluated as a plug-in on three different REC architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, GroundingDINO) and two backbones (Swin-T, Swin-B), with consistent improvements in most settings and new SOTA results on REC-8K.

Thorough ablation studies: the paper isolates the contribution of (a) image-space vs image-text CL vs both combined (Table 3), (b) positive selection strategy via Bipartite Matching vs alternatives (Table 4a), and (c) the positives-only anchor modification of the SupCon loss (Table 4b). These directly support each design decision.

Generality is demonstrated beyond REC via a simple adaptation to class-agnostic counting on FSC-147, and the paper additionally contextualizes against a modern VLM (Molmo2-4B), showing REC remains hard for foundation models.

Fair baseline handling is mostly transparent: the authors state which results come from released checkpoints vs their retraining, and report the alternate CAD-GD inference strategy (CAD-GD†) to avoid unfair comparisons.

The supplementary includes extensive additional qualitative results and honest failure cases (Fig. 8), acknowledging that C-REX models sometimes get the count right while selecting the wrong instances.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially the supervised contrastive loss of Khosla et al. [35] applied to image tokens, with two relatively small changes—positives defined via bipartite matching to GT points, and using only positives as anchors. The framing as a new 'framework' overstates the contribution; this is closer to an empirical finding/loss engineering than a fundamentally new algorithm.

Main REC evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (REC-8K), and the headline 'up to 28% MAE' improvement is driven largely by one baseline (GroundingREC); other comparisons show more modest gains.

Results are not uniformly positive, which the paper does not fully discuss: with CAD-GD†, C-REX slightly degrades validation MAE/RMSE (4.65→4.70, 12.87→13.78); on FSC-147, GroundingREC+C-REX test MAE is notably worse (10.12→12.46); and on paraphrased REs, CAD-GD+C-REX underperforms its baseline. These inconsistencies weaken the generality claims and deserve analysis rather than brief mention.

Potential false negatives in the contrastive objective are not analyzed: background tokens and tokens of unannotated target-class objects are pushed away from positives, which could harm representations in dense or partially annotated scenes; the paper only briefly asserts this is not observed without deeper investigation.
No evidence of statistical robustness: results appear to be from single training runs with no variance or significance reporting, which matters given the magnitude of some improvements is small.

Clarity issues: the 'Project Page' is empty; details such as the loss weight, temperature τ value, and whether the contrastive loss operates on CLS vs all tokens are relegated to or missing from the supplement; no explicit limitations section; no commitment to code/checkpoint release, hurting reproducibility (CAD-GD results depend on the authors' retraining).
The claim that C-REX applies to 'any REC architecture' is supported only for detection/token-based models; applicability to density-based REC methods is untested.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: moving contrastive supervision from the poorly aligned image-text space into the visual embedding space addresses a real weakness of prior REC methods (GroundingREC, CAD-GD), and Section 3.1 articulates the argument (scarcity of negative REs, image-text misalignment) clearly.

The method is a genuine plug-in: it is validated on three different architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, GroundingDINO) and two backbones (Swin-T, Swin-B), with consistent gains in MAE, RMSE, and F1, which supports the generality claim.

Useful ablations are provided: comparison of image-text vs image-space vs combined CL (Table 3), positive sample selection strategies (Table 4a), and the positives-only anchor modification of the supervised contrastive loss (Table 4b), giving the reader a reasonable picture of what drives the gains.
Additional analyses (paraphrase robustness, comparison to Molmo2-4B, class-agnostic extension on FSC-147) and extensive qualitative results with failure cases strengthen the empirical story.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is essentially the supervised contrastive loss of Khosla et al. applied to image tokens with positives determined by bipartite matching, plus a simple modification (using only positives as anchors). Image-space CL is a well-established tool, and the paper itself concedes it 'has been used with great effectiveness in multiple different visual tasks'. The contribution amounts to re-tuning a known loss for a specific task, which is a somewhat thin algorithmic contribution even for a systems-style paper.

Claims are overstated relative to evidence in places. The text asserts C-REX 'consistently improves performance across all architectures and both evaluation metrics' in the class-agnostic setting (Table 2), yet GroundingREC + C-REX degrades on the test set (MAE 12.46 vs 10.12; RMSE 104.53 vs 107.19), and on FSC-147 the improvements are marginal for CAD-GD (13.86 vs 13.80 val MAE). Similarly, in the paraphrase robustness experiment (Table 5a) CAD-GD + C-REX is clearly worse than the baseline, and in Table 1 CAD-GD† beats CAD-GD + C-REX on val RMSE — these are not honestly surfaced in the abstract/introduction framing of 'up to 28% improvement'.

Evaluation rests almost entirely on a single REC benchmark (REC-8K), introduced by the same line of work being improved. There is no second REC dataset to confirm that the findings generalize, and the FSC-147 results are comparatively weak support for the generality claim.

The causal story is not fully disentangled. Because the RE is still used to condition tokens and the bipartite matching relies on ground-truth point supervision at training time, it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the change in contrastive space per se versus simply adding an extra, well-targeted discriminative loss that the baselines did not have in the GroundingDINO case. Table 3 helps but only covers two architectures.

Presentation issues reduce polish: the 'Project Page:' field on page 1 is empty, and the two figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 2) largely repeat the same message. The writing also contains unsupported comparative claims (e.g., CLIP vs DINOv2 analogy in Sec. 3.1) that are used as motivation but not directly tested in this paper's setting.
No discussion of limitations beyond count-range token scarcity, and no societal-impact discussion; given REC's surveillance/crowd-analysis use cases this would have been appropriate.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: shifting contrastive supervision from the poorly aligned image-text space to the visual embedding space, where negatives are abundant (image tokens) rather than scarce (candidate referring expressions). The motivation in Sections 1 and 3.1 is convincing and well supported by prior literature on contrastive learning.

Comprehensive empirical validation: the method is tested as a plug-in on three distinct REC architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, GroundingDINO) and two backbones (Swin-T, Swin-B), with consistent gains in most settings and new state-of-the-art results on REC-8K (e.g., GroundingDINO + C-REX: MAE 4.20 / F1 0.78 on test). The GroundingDINO baseline, which had no contrastive loss at all, is a useful control showing the added objective helps.

Thorough ablation studies: image-text vs image-space vs combined CL (Table 3), positive-sample selection strategy (Table 4a), and the modified supervised contrastive loss using positives-only anchors (Table 4b). Each design decision is empirically justified rather than merely asserted.

Generality is demonstrated beyond REC via a class-agnostic counting adaptation on FSC-147, and the comparison with Molmo2-4B (Table 5b) provides useful context that REC remains challenging for general VLMs.

Honest reporting of negative or mixed results, e.g., CAD-GD performing better under paraphrased REs (Table 5a) and failure cases in the supplementary (Figure 8), which increases the credibility of the evaluation.

The paper is clearly written, with a logical structure from motivation (Figures 1-2) to method (Equations 1-2) to experiments, and a well-organized supplementary with implementation details and extensive qualitative results.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is an adaptation of the supervised contrastive loss (Khosla et al.) to image tokens with positives-only anchors, combined with bipartite matching for label assignment. These are known components combined in a reasonable way; the novelty is primarily in the task-specific design rather than a new learning principle. This does not invalidate the contribution, but it bounds its significance.

The claim of 'consistent improvements across models, backbones and metrics' (Section 4.3) is slightly overstated. In Table 1, CAD-GD† with C-REX has a marginally worse validation MAE than the baseline (4.70 vs 4.65), and in Table 2, GroundingREC + C-REX degrades on the FSC-147 test MAE (10.12 to 12.46). The paper should more precisely characterize where gains hold and where they do not.

No statistical reliability analysis: all results appear to be single training runs without error bars, seeds, or significance tests, despite some reported deltas being small (e.g., class-agnostic counting improvements of ~0.3-0.4 MAE). This weakens several quantitative claims.

The central mechanistic claim—more compact intra-class clusters and better inter-class separation in the visual embedding space (Figures 1-2)—is asserted but never directly visualized (e.g., t-SNE/UMAP of token embeddings with and without C-REX), so the 'right embedding space' framing remains largely inferential from downstream metrics.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the Project Page is empty and no code release is stated. Some baseline comparisons mix released checkpoints (GroundingREC) with retrained models (CAD-GD), which is handled transparently but introduces potential confounds in fairness of comparison.

No dedicated limitations or societal-impact discussion in the main text; failure behavior is only touched on via supplementary qualitative examples. Dense-scene behavior is discussed briefly but the reduced negative-pool effect is dismissed without quantitative analysis.
Improvement magnitudes in class-agnostic counting are small and mixed across architectures, so the claim that C-REX 'extends naturally' to other counting tasks is only modestly supported.
